newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya business hails reformist budget.
newsitem.headline: Kenya business hails reformist budget.

text.p: Kenyan business on Friday hailed Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's state budget as progressive after he stuck to the theme of continued economic reconstruction amid political tensions ahead of general elections this year.
"It represents a continuation. It is pleasing to see Mudavadi sticking to reformist policies," said Roger Bebbington, managing partner at business advisers Coopers & Lybrand.
"We feel that the reforms and the budget themes are absolutely correct," Bebbington told Reuters.

Robin Cahill, of business advisers KPMG Peat Marwick, called the budget conciliatory in an election year. He saw Mudavadi-led reforms as receiving rave reviews from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and Western bilateral donors.
Business and economic experts had feared that Mudavadi would abandon reforms for a "feel-good" budget to please Kenyans across the board ahead of presidential and parliamentary polls.

Mudavadi read his speech amid the most chaotic scenes seen in Kenya's parliament chamber. Opposition members of parliament calling for constitutional reforms disrupted his budget speech before a punch-up with MPs of the ruling KANU party.
Mudavadi called the experience traumatic and unfortunate.

Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) Chairman Jimnah Mbaru said Mudavadi had responded directly to private sector appeals for better conditions for economic growth with initiatives to improve infrastructure more rapidly and to encourage trading on the bourse.
"It was a very progressive budget, building on foundations of macroeconomic, trade and privatisation reforms. He is moving in the right direction," Mbaru told Reuters.
Bebbington said there was some frustration from business at the (slow) pace of the application of the reforms. He added that economic growth figures and forecasts were disappointing.
Mudavadi saw gross domestic growth (GDP) at 4.0 percent in 1997 from 4.6 percent in 1996 and 4.8 percent in 1995. Mudavadi forecast growth at 6.0 percent in 1999.
Local businesses were concerned that Mudavadi did not take any specific measures to reduce high interest rates.

They said that because the budget played down the question, Kenya would remain an attractive destination for foreign investors who see rates on benchmark 91-day treasury bills as highly attractive. But they added such investment did nothing to protect or stimulate small businesses.
Rates on 91-day t-bills stand at around 20 percent.

But Kip Kapur of Barclays Merchant Bank said: "It could be positive in the sense that all this interest in Kenya as an emerging market portrays Kenya well and is likely to attract foreign funds (outside of portfolio investments)."
Mudavadi scrapped a 35 percent capital gains tax imposed on insurance companies listed on the Nairobi Stock Exchange and removed stamp duty on primary issues to encourage growth.
He pledged reforms in telecommunications, railways and roads to improve the business environment. He also streamlined taxes and reduced the top-rate taxes for individuals and corporations.

He estimated gross total expenditure at 192.378 billion shillings ($3.5 billion) in the year ending July 1998 compared to revenues, including foreign grants, of 185.92 billion. That would result in a budget deficit of around 6.458 billion.
Figures he issued showed gross total expenditure at 180.227 billion shillings in 1996/97 compared to revenues of 169.575 billion shillings, giving a deficit of 10.65 billion.
--Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261. ($ = 54.75 Kenyan Shillings)
